Every named block on this site is framed by the extension, so this page is its own demonstration.
The site sets:

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
extensions:
  code-window:
    style: macos
    auto-filename: false
```

## Naming the window

Quarto's `filename` attribute names it:

````markdown
```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
project:
  type: website
```
````

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
project:
  type: website
```

A block with no `filename` is left alone here, because this site turns `auto-filename` off.
With it on, that same block is framed and labelled with its language, in HTML and under Typst alike.

## Deriving the name

With `auto-filename` on, a block that names no file is labelled after its language:

````markdown
```python
print("hello")
```
````

The title bar then reads `PYTHON`.
A derived name is drawn smaller and in capitals, so a reader can tell it from a file that exists on disk.
A block with no language at all is labelled `DEFAULT`, and a block whose language Pandoc cannot highlight keeps its own token as the label.

This section shows source only.
The site sets `auto-filename: false`, so it frames no block that leaves `filename` out.
A single block opts out where the option is on:

````markdown
```{.python code-window-no-auto-filename="true"}
print("hello")
```
````

The attribute only suppresses a derived name.
It cannot ask for one, so `code-window-no-auto-filename="false"` reads exactly like leaving the attribute out.

## The three styles

````markdown
```{.r filename="analysis.R" code-window-style="macos"}
```
````

```{.r filename="analysis.R" code-window-style="macos"}
summary(cars)
```

```{.r filename="analysis.R" code-window-style="windows"}
summary(cars)
```

```{.r filename="analysis.R" code-window-style="default"}
summary(cars)
```

Traffic lights, title-bar buttons, and a plain filename.

## Folding

````markdown
```{.python filename="long.py" code-window-collapse="closed"}
```
````

```{.python filename="long.py" code-window-collapse="closed"}
for i in range(100):
    print(i)
```

```{.python filename="short.py" code-window-collapse="open"}
print("expanded by default")
```

`closed` and `open` differ only in the initial state.
The `<details>` element is built at page load by the script the extension injects, so the fold needs JavaScript; without it the block renders open and unframed.

Set `collapse` under `extensions.code-window` to fold every block, and `code-window-collapse="false"` to opt one out.

## Highlighted lines

A block that highlights lines gets a chip beside its filename:

````markdown
```{.r filename="steps.R" code-line-numbers="2-3"}
```
````

```{.r filename="steps.R" code-line-numbers="2-3"}
x <- seq_len(10)
y <- x^2
z <- sum(y)
z
```

`code-window-lines` writes the chip on its own and leaves Quarto's highlighting alone:

````markdown
```{.r filename="notes.R" code-window-lines="1,4"}
```
````

```{.r filename="notes.R" code-window-lines="1,4"}
x <- seq_len(10)
y <- x^2
z <- sum(y)
z
```

The chip above reads `L1,4`, and no line is highlighted.
Under Typst the same block prints `1,4` in the chip, without the leading `L`.

`lines-label: false` under `extensions.code-window` removes the chip from every block.

## Leaving a block alone

````markdown
```{.bash code-window-enabled="false"}
```
````

```{.bash code-window-enabled="false"}
echo "no chrome on this one"
```

Annotations still render on a block with the chrome turned off.

## Turning the filter off

`enabled` stops the filter for a whole document or project:

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
extensions:
  code-window:
    enabled: false
```

The filter still checks each block's attributes against its schema.
It then adds no chrome to any block, and loads neither the stylesheet nor the script.
So `code-window-enabled="true"` on a block cannot switch the chrome back on.
`code-window-enabled` can only turn a block off, never on.

Switching the filter off does not put the document back exactly as Quarto would write it.
The pass that normalises a block's language runs either way, so a block with no language still gains the `default` class.

A block that names a file still gets the plain title bar Quarto builds for it.
That bar carries no traffic lights, no fold, and no line chip.

See [Options](reference.qmd#options) for the option and [Per-block attributes](reference.qmd#per-block-attributes) for the attribute.

## The output of an executed cell

An engine writes the output of a cell as a code block with no language, inside a `cell-output` div.
The filter leaves that block as Quarto wrote it:

````markdown
::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1 4 9 16
```

:::
````

`cell-output: true` frames it instead.
The frame comes from the derived name, so `auto-filename` has to be on as well.
The title bar then reads `DEFAULT`, because the output block carries no language of its own.
This site turns `auto-filename` off, so `cell-output: true` adds no frame here.

With `cell-output` off, which is the default, the extension marks every block inside a `cell-output` div and then leaves it alone, so the output keeps the shape Quarto gives it.
Only `cell-output: true` lets the rest of the extension touch those blocks.

An engine can name the output instead, through knitr's `attr-output` for example.
Output named that way is framed whatever `cell-output` says:

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```{.default filename="console"}
[1] 1 4 9 16
```

:::

This page runs no engine, so the div above is written by hand in the shape an engine produces.
See [Executed cells](reference.qmd#executed-cells) for the option itself.

## Renaming the Typst function

Under Typst the chrome is a call to a function the extension writes into the document.
`wrapper` renames that function and the helper functions beside it:

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
extensions:
  code-window:
    wrapper: "my-window"
```

Each block then emits `#my-window(...)` in place of `#code-window(...)`, and the annotation helpers become `my-window-annotation-item` and `my-window-circled-number`.
Rename it when the document already defines a function called `code-window`.
The option does nothing in HTML, which draws its chrome from the stylesheet and the script instead.

## The Typst hot-fixes

The three hot-fixes act on Typst output only.
Each one is on by default.
A boolean turns one off:

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
extensions:
  code-window:
    hotfix:
      code-annotations: true
      skylighting: false
      typst-title: true
```

A map adds a version at which the hot-fix switches itself off:

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
extensions:
  code-window:
    hotfix:
      skylighting:
        enabled: true
        quarto-version: "1.9.0"
```

The extension compares that string with the running Quarto.
At or above the named version the hot-fix stays out, whatever `enabled` says.
An upgrade thus retires the hot-fix with no further edit.

Two pairs are linked.

`code-annotations` and `skylighting` work together: the first resolves the annotations, and the second supplies the rule that draws the circled marker beside an annotated line.
Turn `skylighting` off, and the numbered list stays under the block while every marker inside it goes, along with the block styling and the inline code backgrounds the same module supplies.

`typst-title` follows `enabled`: with the filter off, theorem titles stay as Quarto writes them.

See [Hot-fixes](reference.qmd#hot-fixes) for what each one corrects.
